programs.nl_rule:
a few scattered colored cells on a unicolored background.

there is a unique center of the colored cells, to which each colored cell has a diagonal offset. move diagonally from each colored cell until you are one cell away from the unique center cell. This cell is colored in the color of the starting cell. The unique center cell is colored grey.

The input and output grid have the same shape.

content.text:
Let me understand the rule from the verifier.

The verifier finds colored cells (nonzero). It finds the row with the most colored cells (k), gets the leftmost cols a and rightmost b. c = center column = (a+b)//2, d = (b-a)//2. Then candidates center rows are k-d and k+d. It picks the first candidate where every colored cell satisfies |ri - cand_r| == |ci - c| (i.e., all colored cells are on diagonals from the center).

Then it sets grid[center_r][center_c] = 5 (grey). Then for each colored cell, computes sign of dr and dc, and if both nonzero (diagonal), adds a cell at center_r + s_dr, center_c + s_dc with that color (if empty).

So essentially: find the unique center. Each colored cell moves diagonally toward the center until one cell away from center. That cell is colored with the starting cell's color. Center becomes grey.

Wait, but note only one cell per diagonal direction is added. So if multiple colored cells on the same diagonal direction... only the closest one matters? Actually the code iterates all colored cells but only adds at the one-cell-away-from-center position. So the position added is (center_r ± 1, center_c ± 1), the 4 diagonal neighbors of center. Multiple colored cells in the same diagonal direction would write to the same cell, last one wins in iteration order. Hmm.

But for teaching, I should just show examples. Let me just verify the given example matches.

Input: colored cells: (2,9,1), (10,1,8), (10,9,2). Let's compute. row_count: row2:1, row10:2. max_count=2, k=10. cols_list=[1,9]. a=1,b=9,c=5,d=4. Candidates r1=10-4=6, r2=10+4=14 (out of range). So center_r=6? Check each colored: (2,9): |2-6|=4, |9-5|=4 ok. (10,1): |10-6|=4,|1-5|=4 ok. (10,9): |10-6|=4,|9-5|=4 ok. center=(6,5). grid[6][5]=5. Then for (2,9): dr=2-6=-4 s=-1, dc=9-5=4 s=+1, add at (6-1,5+1)=(5,6) color1. For (10,1): dr=+4 s=+1, dc=-4 s=-1, add at (7,4) color 8. For (10,9): dr=(10-6)=+4 s=+1, dc=+4 s=+1, add at (7,6) color 2. This matches output: (5,6)=1, (7,4)=8, (7,6)=2, (6,5)=5. Yes.

Now I need to teach the Student. I'll show a couple examples to convey the rule. Note the student learns from demonstrations. Complexity: the shape varies. Let me create a few examples with different arrangements.

Important caveat: the verifier's center-finding depends on the row with the most colored cells. Usually colored cells cluster such that the center is well-defined. Let me build simple examples.

Actually, simpler: produce examples of the general pattern. Let me design an input where colored cells are on diagonals from center. E.g., center at (5,5) in an 11x11 grid. Colored cells: place at diagonal corners.

Let me just make input with colored cells at (3,3,3), (3,7,4), (7,3,6), (7,7,7)? But then rows each have 2 colored cells → row_count ties. max() picks... row_count.get for keys; keys order 3,7. max returns first max encountered? Actually max with key over dict iterates keys; first max is key 3 (if equal). k=3, cols_list for row 3 = [3,7], a=3,b=7,c=5,d=2. Candidates r1=3-2=1, r2=3+2=5. Check center (5,5)? For colored (3,3): |3-cand_r| == |3-5|=2. cand_r=1: |3-1|=2 ok, |3-5|=2 ok. cand_r=1 valid check all: (7,3): |7-1|=6 vs |3-5|=2 no. So cand_r=1 fails. cand_r=5: (3,3): |3-5|=2=|3-5| ok; (7,3): |7-5|=2=|3-5|=?? wait |ci-c|=|3-5|=2, ok. (3,7): |3-5|=2, |7-5|=2 ok. (7,7): 2,2 ok. So center (5,5). 

Output: center (5,5)=5. For each: (3,3): dr=-2 s=-1, dc=-2 s=-1 → (4,4) color3. (3,7): dr=-1,dc=+1→(4,6) color4. (7,3): (6,4) color6. (7,7): (6,6) color7. Nice.

But hypotheses: student might think it's just the 4 diagonal neighbors of center with colors determined somehow. That's basically right for this. But the real task has more than 4 cells sometimes. Hmm, but each cell maps to one of 4 diagonal neighbors. So the output has at most 4 colored cells around the center. The colors are determined by which colored cell is on that diagonal direction (the one closest? Actually any cell in that direction, and multiple could conflict, last wins).

Actually wait — the added cell is always at exactly one step diagonally from center. So all added cells are the 4 diagonal neighbors. Multiple input colored cells in same quadrant all map to the same output cell; iteration order determines which color wins. In practice probably exactly one per quadrant.

So the student must figure out: from scattered colored cells, find center (via diagonals), color center grey (5), and place each colored cell's color at the diagonal neighbor of the center in the direction from center to that cell.

The tricky part is finding the center. Let me give examples with varying sizes and number of cells.

tools.name: show_example

input_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

output_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

tools.description: Show the Student a labeled input-output pair that you authored. If your output matches the rule, the pair is shown and you receive a success acknowledgement only. If it does not match, the pair is not shown and you receive the gold output so you can correct it.

tools.name: show_transformed_input

input_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

tools.description: Provide only an input grid. The environment applies the verifier and shows the resulting gold input-output pair to the student.

tools.name: query_student

input_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

tools.description: Probe the student with an input of your choice. You receive the student's predicted output, the gold output, and whether they matched. The student does not see the gold pair unless you later show it with show_example or show_transformed_input.

tools.name: start_exam
tools.description: End teaching and send the student to the exam: they must solve held-out generator inputs (unseen in demonstrations or probes) with the history so far. No further teaching after this.

Hmm order: first sets center grey if empty, then adds adjacents. If a colored cell is diagonal at distance 1 from center... but colored cells include... wait center is determined by symmetry, and colored cell at center? The center is derived and then check all colored have |dr|==|dc|. A cell at the center has dr=dc=0, valid. Then s_dr=0, skipped. So center cell if colored stays.

Edge cases with a colored cell adjacent to center: then add_r,add_c = center coords (since dr=±1 → s_dr = dr, add = center+dr... wait add_r = center_r + s_dr, and s_dr is sign of dr, so if dr=1, s_dr=1, add_r=center_r+1=ri. Actually add = the cell itself. So it would try to color the cell's own position, already colored. Fine.
